title: How does a token bucket let a burst through but refuse a flood?
answer: A burst can spend only the tokens saved up, and only elapsed time adds more

checks.question: At 4 tokens a second, R9 leaves 1 token and R10 arrives four seconds later. How many tokens does R10 find, and why not 17?
checks.answer: Five. Four seconds at 4 a second would add 16, but min(5, …) stops the balance at the bucket’s five and throws the rest away.

checks.question: At 2 tokens a second, R8 and R9 arrive at the same instant. Why does R8 get 200 and R9 get 429?
checks.answer: The half second since R7 added exactly one token, and R8 spent it. No time passes between R8 and R9, so nothing is added and R9 finds 0.

checks.question: At 1 token a second, what does R7 find half a second after the burst?
checks.answer: Half a token: 0.5 s × 1 a second. That is less than the one token a request needs, so R7 gets 429.

steps.title: Ten requests from one client, and a bucket of five tokens
steps.line: Predict: R1–R6 arrive at the same instant. How many get 200?
steps.caption: A server shares its work among many clients, so it limits each one: a request it serves gets 200, OK, and one it refuses gets 429, Too Many Requests, which tells the client to slow down. A short burst should still get through. So the server keeps a balance of tokens for the client, at most five: the bucket. Each accepted request spends one token; a request that finds less than one gets 429. Capacity sets the burst the client can save; refill rate sets how quickly it earns another request. The dashed line marks the one token a request needs. How many of six simultaneous requests can spend this balance?
steps.picture: Bucket balance: 5 tokens left, last refill at 0 seconds, 0 accepted; rejected requests: none; The bucket, filled to 5.0 of 5 tokens; A chart of tokens, 0 to 5, against time, 0 to 5 s, with a dashed line at the one token a request needs; Requests R1 to R10 at their arrival times: none answered yet; Code “bucket.allow(now), rate = 1”, 8 lines. Refill: 2: tokens = min(5; 3: tokens + (now - lastRefill) * rate); 4: lastRefill = now.

steps.title: Answer: five 200s, then a 429
steps.line: Predict: R7 arrives half a second later, at 0.5 s. 200 or 429?
steps.caption: No time passed between R1 and R6, so the line drops one token per request and R6 finds 0.0, under the dashed line: 429. A burst can spend only the tokens saved up, and only elapsed time adds more. On each arrival the server adds elapsed time multiplied by the refill rate, here 1 token a second, before deciding whether to spend a token. The line between arrivals shows available credit; no background timer needs to update the balance.

steps.title: Answer: 429. R7 finds 0.5 tokens after half a second
steps.line: R8 at 1 s finds 1.0; R9 at the same instant finds what R8 left.
steps.caption: Between calls the line climbs 1 token a second. Half a second after the burst, R7 finds 0.5 tokens, less than the one a request needs, so it gets 429. The rate decides it: the same half second buys 0.5 tokens at 1 a second (429), 1.0 token at 2 a second (200) and 2.0 tokens at 4 a second (200). R8 at 1 s finds 1.0; R9 arrives at the same instant, so nothing is added and it finds what R8 left. Fractional tokens are saved, but a request must spend a whole one. R7 (0.5) and R9 (0.0) are under the dashed line, so they get 429.

steps.title: R10 waits 4 s and finds 4 tokens
steps.line: The line climbs to 4.0, under the cap of five.
steps.caption: R9 left 0, and a wait of 4 s at 1 token a second brings the balance to 4, under min(5, …)'s cap. R10 spends one and leaves 3. At 2 tokens a second and 4 tokens a second the same wait would pass five, and min(5, …) would stop the balance there.

steps.title: The same ten requests at 1, 2 and 4 tokens a second
steps.line: 429s at 4 / s: R6; at 1 / s: R6, R7 and R9.
steps.caption: Each row runs the same ten requests at its labelled refill rate; the outlined row is this case. Circles are 200s and crosses are 429s. R6 is refused at every rate, because no time passes inside the burst, and R10 is accepted at every rate, because after its 4-second wait it finds at least 4 tokens. In between, the rate decides: at 4 tokens a second, R6 gets 429; at 1 token a second, R6, R7 and R9 do.
